shots.B03C288S01H01: Ravana's illusions fail, Matali brings Indra's chariot, and Rama fires a Brahma weapon that burns Ravana to nothing.

B03C289.summary: With Ravana dead, the gods honor Rama, who gives Lanka to Vibhishana. Rama then coldly doubts Sita's purity, and she is crushed; the gods, Brahma and Dasaratha among them, declare her innocent, so Rama takes her back. Rama returns to Ayodhya on the Pushpaka chariot, is reunited with Bharata, is crowned, and performs ten horse-sacrifices. The section closes the Ramayana episode with the restoration of Rama's family and kingdom.

scenes.B03C289S01: Ravana is slain, the gods praise Rama, Sita's purity is affirmed, Rama returns to Ayodhya, and he is crowned and performs the sacrifices.

shots.B03C289S01H01: The gods and sages honor Rama and celebrate after Ravana is slain.
shots.B03C289S01H02: Rama gives Lanka to Vibhishana, then harshly doubts Sita's chastity; Sita calls on the elements to witness her innocence, and the gods, including Brahma and Dasaratha, declare her pure and urge Rama to take her back.
shots.B03C289S01H03: Dasaratha tells Rama the fourteen years of exile are over, Rama rewards Avindhya and Trijata, asks Brahma to restore the slain monkeys to life, and Sita blesses Hanuman with long life.
shots.B03C289S01H04: The gods leave, Rama flies home on the Pushpaka with Sita and his allies, installs Angada as prince-regent, is reunited with Bharata, is crowned at Ayodhya, sends his allies home, returns the chariot, and performs ten horse-sacrifices.

B03C290.summary: Markandeya consoles Yudhishthira by pointing out that Rama and other heroes also endured hardship and that Yudhishthira has powerful brothers and allies. He urges the king to stop grieving and act as a warrior should. Yudhishthira is comforted and speaks again to Markandeya. The passage links Rama's trials to the Pandavas' own exile.

scenes.B03C290S01: Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Rama also suffered, that the Pandavas have strong allies, and that he should not grieve.

shots.B03C290S01H01: Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Rama also suffered, that a warrior must act rather than mourn, and that his brothers and allies such as Dhananjaya, Bhima and the twins make victory likely, so he should not grieve.
shots.B03C290S01H02: Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira was comforted and then spoke again to Markandeya.

B03C291.summary: Yudhishthira says he grieves most for Draupadi, who once saved the brothers at the dice game and was carried off by Jayadratha, and asks whether Markandeya knows a more faithful lady. Markandeya begins the tale of Savitri, daughter of the Madra king Aswapati, who was born through a boon from the goddess Savitri after years of devotion. The girl grows beautiful, and when no suitor comes forward, her father tells her to choose a husband herself. The section introduces the theme of a wife's devotion.

scenes.B03C291S01: Yudhishthira asks about faithful wives, and Markandeya tells how Aswapati's daughter Savitri was born and grew up unmarried.
scenes.B03C291S02: Savitri sets out with her father's counsellors to travel the holy places and search for a husband.

shots.B03C291S01H01: Heading marking the Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, a section on the glory of devoted wives.
shots.B03C291S01H02: Yudhishthira says he grieves most for Draupadi, who saved them at the dice game and was carried off by Jayadratha, and asks whether Markandeya has known a more faithful lady.
shots.B03C291S01H03: Markandeya tells how King Aswapati of the Madras, without children, prayed for eighteen years, and the goddess Savitri promised him a daughter.
shots.B03C291S01H04: The daughter is born to the king's eldest queen, is named Savitri, and grows so beautiful that no suitor dares ask for her hand.
shots.B03C291S01H05: Aswapati tells his grown daughter to find her own husband, warning that a father who does not give his daughter in marriage falls into disgrace.
shots.B03C291S02H01: Savitri, with her father's old counsellors, travels to the forest hermitages, serves the elders and gives gifts at holy places in her search for a husband.

B03C292.summary: Narada visits King Aswapati, who asks where his daughter has been. Savitri names Satyavan, son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena, and Narada praises his virtues. Narada then warns that Satyavan is fated to die within a year, but Savitri refuses to choose another man, and Narada approves the match. Aswapati accepts and prepares the wedding, setting up Satyavan's early death and Savitri's devotion.

scenes.B03C292S01: Savitri names Satyavan as her choice, Narada warns that he will die within a year, Savitri holds to her choice, and her father begins the wedding preparations.

shots.B03C292S01H01: Savitri returns from her travels and finds her father with Narada, who asks where she has been and whom she has chosen.
shots.B03C292S01H02: Savitri names Satyavan, son of the blind, exiled Dyumatsena; Narada praises him but warns he will die within a year, and Savitri refuses to choose another, so Narada gives his approval and leaves.
shots.B03C292S01H03: Narada rises into the sky and departs, and Aswapati begins to prepare his daughter's wedding.

B03C293.summary: King Aswapati brings Savitri to the hermitage of the blind, exiled Dyumatsena and asks that she be married to Satyavan. Dyumatsena hesitates because of their poverty, but Aswapati insists and the wedding is held with due rites. Savitri lives in the hermitage as a devoted wife, pleasing everyone, but Narada's warning never leaves her mind. The section sets up the fated death that will test her.

scenes.B03C293S01: Aswapati asks Dyumatsena for Satyavan's hand, the wedding is held in the hermitage, and Savitri lives there as a devoted wife, still troubled by Narada's warning.

shots.B03C293S01H01: Aswapati visits Dyumatsena's hermitage, asks that Savitri be accepted as Satyavan's wife, and Dyumatsena, after noting their hardship, agrees.
shots.B03C293S01H02: The wedding is performed with rites, Savitri serves her husband and in-laws devotedly and pleases them all, but Narada's words stay in her mind day and night.

B03C294.summary: The fated day arrives. Savitri, who has counted the days, observes a three-night fast and receives the hermitage's blessing that she will never be widowed. When Satyavan goes into the forest with his axe, she insists on going with him despite her fast, and her in-laws give permission. She walks beside him through the woods, grieving and expecting his death at that hour. The scene builds the suspense that drives the next part of the story.

scenes.B03C294S01: The day of Satyavan's fated death arrives, Savitri completes her fast and insists on following him into the forest, and she goes with him, grieving.

shots.B03C294S01H01: Savitri, who has counted the days to the death Narada foretold, keeps a three-night fast, and after her morning rites, the hermitage ascetics bless her that she will never be widowed.
shots.B03C294S01H02: Her in-laws tell her to eat, but she answers that she will eat only after sunset, as her vow requires.
shots.B03C294S01H03: Satyavan takes his axe and sets out for the forest, and Savitri insists on going with him despite her fast, while he warns her of the hard paths.
shots.B03C294S01H04: Savitri asks her in-laws for leave to go into the forest with her husband, and Dyumatsena grants it.
shots.B03C294S01H05: Savitri walks with Satyavan through the woods, smiling outwardly while grieving, and, remembering Narada's words, watches him closely, expecting his death at that moment.

B03C295.summary: In the forest Satyavan falls ill from head pain and dies in Savitri's lap when Yama comes to take him. Savitri follows Yama and, through a series of replies on duty and righteousness, wins boons: sight and a restored kingdom for Dyumatsena, sons for her father, and a hundred sons for herself and Satyavan. Yama then restores Satyavan's life, and the couple sets out for the hermitage at night. The section is the turning point of Savitri's tale, showing her wisdom and devotion.

scenes.B03C295S01: Satyavan falls ill and dies in Savitri's lap, Savitri wins Yama's boons and Satyavan's life back, and the couple starts home through the night.

shots.B03C295S01H01: Satyavan, with head pain from chopping wood, lays his head in Savitri's lap, and she sees Yama in red standing beside him with a noose and learns that Yama has come to take her husband.
shots.B03C295S01H02: Yama draws Satyavan's life out of his body and Savitri follows him; her replies on righteousness win her boons for Dyumatsena's sight and kingdom, sons for her father, and a century of sons, before she asks for Satyavan's life.
shots.B03C295S01H03: Yama frees Satyavan, promises him a long life and many sons, and departs, and Satyavan wakes in Savitri's lap.
shots.B03C295S01H04: Satyavan, recovered, recalls his vision and worries about his blind father and aged mother, and Savitri urges him to rest and wait for morning, though he insists on going home.
shots.B03C295S01H05: Savitri takes the axe and wallet and supports Satyavan, and he guides them along the path to the north toward the hermitage, eager to see his parents.

B03C296.summary: Dyumatsena regains his sight and searches the hermitages for his lost son, while the sages assure him that Satyavan must be alive. Satyavan and Savitri return at night, and Savitri explains how she won Yama's boons, including Satyavan's life. The sages praise her for rescuing the family's fortunes. The story ends Savitri's test and shows the reward of her devotion.

scenes.B03C296S01: Dyumatsena searches for Satyavan, the couple returns, Savitri explains her boons, and the sages praise her and leave.

shots.B03C296S01H01: Dyumatsena, now able to see, searches the hermitages with his wife Saivya, and each sage assures him that Satyavan must still be alive, giving his reasons.
shots.B03C296S01H02: Satyavan and Savitri come back at night; Satyavan describes his sleep, the sages ask what happened, and Savitri explains Yama's boons, which the sages hail as rescuing the family.
shots.B03C296S01H03: The sages praise Savitri and bid farewell to the king and his son, and they go home.

B03C297.summary: Messengers from Salwa report that the usurper has been killed by his own minister and invite Dyumatsena back to his throne. He is restored, with Satyavan as prince-regent, and Savitri later bears a hundred sons. Markandeya says Draupadi can likewise rescue the Pandavas. Yudhishthira, encouraged by the tale, continues to live in the Kamyaka forest.

scenes.B03C297S01: Messengers bring Dyumatsena news of the usurper's death and an invitation to return, he is restored to the throne, and the tale closes with Markandeya's words to Yudhishthira.

shots.B03C297S01H01: Messengers from Salwa report the usurper's death and invite Dyumatsena back, he is installed on the throne with Satyavan as prince-regent, Savitri bears a hundred sons, and Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Draupadi, like Savitri, will rescue them.
shots.B03C297S01H02: Vaisampayana says that encouraged by the story, Yudhishthira kept living in the Kamyaka forest, and that anyone who hears the tale of Savitri with reverence gains happiness.

B03C298.summary: Janamejaya asks why Yudhishthira feared Karna and why he kept that fear to himself. Vaisampayana explains that in the thirteenth year of exile Indra planned to beg Karna's earrings for the Pandavas, and that Surya warned Karna in a dream. Karna refuses to break his vow of giving, saying fame is worth more than his life. The passage sets up the loss of Karna's protection.

scenes.B03C298S01: Janamejaya asks about Yudhishthira's fear, Vaisampayana explains Indra's plan and Surya's warning, and Karna chooses fame over safety.

shots.B03C298S01H01: Janamejaya asks why Yudhishthira feared Karna and kept the fear hidden, even though Indra had promised through Lomasa to remove it.
shots.B03C298S01H02: Vaisampayana explains that in the thirteenth year of exile Indra resolved to beg Karna's earrings, and Surya came to Karna in a dream disguised as a Brahmana to warn him.
shots.B03C298S01H03: Karna asks who the Brahmana is, and when Surya reveals himself, Karna refuses to break his vow of giving, prefers lasting fame to life, and resolves to give Indra his earrings and armor.

B03C299.summary: Surya urges Karna not to give up his earrings and armor. He argues that fame is of no use to the dead, that Karna should refuse Indra's request, and that with the earrings Karna could not be defeated by Arjuna. The advice shows Surya's protective concern and the stakes of the coming bargain.

scenes.B03C299S01: Surya presses Karna to refuse the earrings, arguing that fame does not help the dead and that the earrings guarantee his strength against Arjuna.

shots.B03C299S01H01: Surya warns Karna that fame is worthless to the dead, urges him to refuse Indra's request for the earrings, and says that with them Karna cannot be beaten by Arjuna.

B03C300.summary: Karna tells Surya that he cannot lie, would rather die than be untruthful, and will give his earrings and armor to any Brahmana who asks. Surya then advises him to demand an infallible dart from Indra in return, since such a dart never misses. Surya vanishes, and Karna tells him of the dream the next morning and waits for Indra's visit. The chapter ends with Karna set on his course.

scenes.B03C300S01: Karna refuses to give up his vow, Surya advises him to ask Indra for a dart in exchange for the earrings, and Karna waits for Indra.

shots.B03C300S01H01: Karna tells Surya he would sooner die than lie, will give his earrings and armor to Brahmanas, and promises to defeat Arjuna in battle anyway.
shots.B03C300S01H02: Surya advises Karna to demand from Indra an infallible dart that never fails to slay enemies as the price for the earrings.
shots.B03C300S01H03: Surya vanishes, Karna tells him of the dream the next morning, Surya confirms it, and Karna waits for Indra to come for the dart.

B03C301.summary: Janamejaya asks what secret Surya kept from Karna and where Karna's earrings and armor came from. Vaisampayana explains that a fierce Brahmana once came to King Kuntibhoja asking to stay as his guest. The king entrusts the Brahmana's care to his adopted daughter Pritha, and the girl is told to serve him with great care. The section opens the story of how Karna was born and why his armor and earrings matter.

scenes.B03C301S01: Janamejaya asks about Karna's earrings, and Vaisampayana begins the story of the Brahmana guest and Kuntibhoja's daughter Pritha.

shots.B03C301S01H01: Janamejaya asks what secret Surya kept from Karna and where Karna's earrings and armor came from.
shots.B03C301S01H02: Vaisampayana says a Brahmana of fierce energy asked King Kuntibhoja to host him as a guest, and the king tells his adopted daughter Pritha to wait on the Brahmana with care.

B03C302.summary: Pritha, now called Kunti, promises the king she will serve the Brahmana faithfully, saying that Brahmanas bring blessings when pleased and ruin when angered. Kuntibhoja gives the Brahmana fine quarters and asks Kunti to forgive any lapses. Kunti then takes up her duty with complete devotion, treating the guest as a god.

scenes.B03C302S01: Kunti promises to serve the Brahmana, her father hands him over to her care, and she waits on him devotedly.

shots.B03C302S01H01: Kunti promises to serve the Brahmana faithfully, her father asks forgiveness for any fault in her, and she attends the guest as if he were a god.

B03C303.summary: Kunti serves the Brahmana for a full year, providing food, bed and seat at all hours, though he often returns late or scolds her. Pleased, the Brahmana offers her a boon, but she says she already has everything she needs. He then teaches her a mantra that can summon any god who will serve her. The episode establishes the mantra that drives the next events.

scenes.B03C303S01: Kunti's service wins the Brahmana's approval, he offers her a boon, and she declines it in favor of a mantra that summons a god.

shots.B03C303S01H01: Kunti serves the Brahmana at all hours through a year without complaint, and when he offers a boon, she declines, and he gives her a mantra to summon any god she wishes.
shots.B03C303S01H02: Fearing his curse, Kunti accepts the mantras, the Brahmana vanishes after saying he is leaving, and Kuntibhoja is amazed.

B03C304.summary: Kunti, curious about the mantra, tests it while she is still unmarried, summoning the rising sun. Surya appears and insists that she yield to him, threatening her and her father with his anger and a curse. Kunti, bewildered by the celestial gods watching, begs him to go away. Surya argues that a maiden has her own freedom and refuses to leave without his purpose.

scenes.B03C304S01: Kunti tests the mantra on the rising sun, Surya appears and demands her, and she begs him to leave, but he refuses.

shots.B03C304S01H01: Kunti tests the mantra by summoning the sun, who appears and tells her that she must yield to him or face his curse, and that the gods are watching.
shots.B03C304S01H02: Kunti begs Surya to leave and says a maiden's body belongs to her father or mother; Surya replies that she is still a girl, that her virginity is hers, and that he will not go away empty-handed.

B03C305.summary: Kunti cannot dissuade Surya, fears for her father and the Brahmana, and finally agrees on condition that her son be born with armor and earrings. Surya promises a son with invulnerable armor and earrings made of Amrita, which he says came from Aditi. He enters her by yoga and leaves her a mother who remains a virgin, and when he departs she regains consciousness. The passage is the birth of Karna, the central tragedy of the Mahabharata.

scenes.B03C305S01: Kunti pleads with Surya, consents on condition that her son have armor and earrings, and is made pregnant by Surya while remaining a virgin.

shots.B03C305S01H01: Kunti fails to dissuade Surya and, weighing the danger to her father and the Brahmana, reflects at length on her dilemma.
shots.B03C305S01H02: Kunti pleads that a son born of an unmarried union would bring disgrace, Surya argues that a maiden is free by nature, and he promises her a son with Amrita armor and earrings, and she consents.
shots.B03C305S01H03: Surya enters Kunti by yoga and touches her navel, leaving her stupefied, and says she will bear a son who will be the best of warriors while remaining a virgin.
shots.B03C305S01H04: Kunti, half-fainting, accepts; Surya places the child in her womb without harming her maidenhood, and she regains consciousness after he has gone.

B03C307.summary: The charioteer Adhiratha and his childless wife Radha find the box in the Ganga, see the golden-armored infant, and adopt him as their son, naming him Vasusena and Vrisha. The boy grows up in the Anga kingdom, is trained by Drona, befriends Duryodhana and becomes a rival of Arjuna. Pritha learns of his life through spies. The section establishes Karna's upbringing and his enmity toward the Pandavas.

scenes.B03C307S01: Adhiratha and Radha adopt the foundling from the river, he is raised as their son, trained as a warrior, and becomes Duryodhana's friend and Arjuna's rival.

shots.B03C307S01H01: The charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha find the box in the Ganga, adopt the golden-armored boy, and raise him as their son, and the boy is later called Vasusena and Vrisha; he is trained by Drona, befriends Duryodhana and challenges Arjuna, while Yudhishthira is troubled by his armor and his rivalry.

B03C308.summary: Indra comes disguised as a Brahmana while Karna is worshipping at noon and asks for his armor and earrings. Karna offers many other gifts, but refuses to give up the armor and earrings that make him unslayable. Indra admits that Surya warned Karna, and in exchange gives an infallible dart. Karna cuts his armor and earrings from his body, earns the name Karna, and Indra departs. The Kauravas are dismayed and the Pandavas rejoice, and the scene turns to the Pandavas returning to Dwaitavana.

scenes.B03C308S01: Indra begs Karna's armor and earrings, Karna refuses every other gift, and he gives them up in exchange for an infallible dart.
scenes.B03C308S02: Janamejaya asks where the Pandavas were, and Vaisampayana says they returned to Dwaitavana after finishing their exile.

shots.B03C308S01H01: Indra in the guise of a Brahmana asks Karna for his armor and earrings, and Karna offers gold, damsels and cattle, but the Brahmana asks for nothing else.
shots.B03C308S01H02: Karna explains that the armor and earrings make him unslayable and offers the whole kingdom instead, but the Brahmana still asks only for the armor and earrings.
shots.B03C308S01H03: Karna says he knew Indra's identity, and Indra admits that Surya had warned Karna and offers him any boon except the thunderbolt.
shots.B03C308S01H04: Karna asks for an infallible dart, and Indra sets its terms: it kills one powerful enemy and then returns to him, while Karna asks that his body not be disfigured and Indra agrees.
shots.B03C308S01H05: Karna cuts off his armor and earrings and gives them to Indra, earning the name Karna; Indra goes to heaven, the Kauravas are dismayed, and the Pandavas rejoice.
shots.B03C308S02H01: Janamejaya asks where the Pandavas were when they heard the news, and what they did when their twelfth year of exile ended.
shots.B03C308S02H02: Vaisampayana says the Pandavas, having defeated Jayadratha, rescued Draupadi, finished their exile, and heard Markandeya's tales, returned from Kamyaka to Dwaitavana with their people.

B03C309.summary: The Pandavas settle in the forest of Dwaitavana. A deer runs off with a Brahmana's fire-sticks and churning staff, and the brothers chase it in vain, growing tired and thirsty. They rest under a banyan tree, and Nakula asks why disaster has come to them, since their house has never abandoned virtue. The section starts a new book on the forest and sets up the trouble ahead.

scenes.B03C309S01: The Pandavas dwell in Dwaitavana, a deer carries off a Brahmana's fire-sticks, and the brothers chase it in vain and rest under a banyan tree.

shots.B03C309S01H01: Heading marking the Aranya Parva, the book of the forest.
shots.B03C309S01H02: Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after their grief over Draupadi's abduction and her rescue.
shots.B03C309S01H03: Vaisampayana says the Pandavas lived at Dwaitavana, and after a deer ran off with a Brahmana's fire-sticks and churning staff, they chased it in vain and sat down exhausted under a banyan, where Nakula asked why disaster had come to them.

B03C306.summary: Pritha, hiding her pregnancy, gives birth to a son who is born with armor and earrings. Fearing disgrace, she sets the child adrift in a box on the river Aswa, praying for his protection. The box drifts down the rivers to the Ganga and reaches the city of Champa, where the child survives because of his armor, earrings and destiny. The episode explains how the future Karna was abandoned at birth.

scenes.B03C306S01: Pritha gives birth in secret, prays over her son, and sends him off in a box on the river Aswa, which drifts to Champa where the child is kept alive.

shots.B03C306S01H01: Pritha secretly gives birth to a son born with armor and earrings, and, weeping and fearing disgrace, places him in a wicker box and prays for his protection as she sets him on the Aswa.
shots.B03C306S01H02: Pritha casts the box into the river at night and returns to the palace, and the box floats on through the Charmanwati, the Yamuna and the Ganga to Champa, where his armor and earrings keep him alive.

B03C310.summary: Weary and thirsty in the forest, the Pandavas reflect on the causes of their misfortunes, each brother blaming a past failure. Yudhishthira sends his brothers one by one to fetch water, and each drinks from a lake without answering an invisible being's questions and falls dead. Bhima too dies after drinking, and Yudhishthira, worried, goes to search and comes upon a beautiful lake. The episode sets up his meeting with the Yaksha at the lake.

scenes.B03C310S01: The brothers reflect on their misfortunes, Yudhishthira sends them for water, each dies at the lake after drinking without answering, and Yudhishthira goes searching and finds the lake.

shots.B03C310S01H01: Yudhishthira says calamity has no clear cause, and Bhima, Arjuna and Sahadeva each blame a past lapse for their misfortune.
shots.B03C310S01H02: Yudhishthira sends Nakula, then Sahadeva and Arjuna, to fetch water, and each drinks from the lake without answering a voice's questions and dies; Bhima also goes, is warned by the same voice, and is about to drink.
shots.B03C310S01H03: Bhima drinks without answering and dies, and Yudhishthira, uneasy at the long delay, searches the forest and comes upon a beautiful lake.

B03C311.summary: Yudhishthira mourns his four dead brothers, recalls the prophecies that promised their success, and wonders who could have killed them. Before drinking, he goes to bathe in the lake, where a Yaksha, disguised as a crane, warns him and claims to have killed the brothers. Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's long run of questions on duty, learning, wealth and conduct, and when offered one brother's life, he chooses Nakula out of fairness to both of his father's wives. The Yaksha is pleased and restores all the brothers. The episode is the Pandavas' great test of wisdom and of fair dealing.

scenes.B03C311S01: Yudhishthira mourns and reflects on his dead brothers, the Yaksha challenges him, and after a long set of answers he chooses Nakula, and all four brothers are restored.

shots.B03C311S01H01: Yudhishthira mourns his four dead brothers, recalls the promises made at their births, wonders who could have killed them, and, going to bathe in the lake, hears a Yaksha say from the sky that he is the one who slew them.
shots.B03C311S01H02: Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's questions one by one on duty, learning, the sun, wealth, friendship and conduct, and when offered one brother's life he chooses Nakula out of fairness to both of his father's wives, so the Yaksha restores all the brothers.

B03C312.summary: The Yaksha reveals himself as Dharma, the Lord of justice and Yudhishthira's father, who had taken the fire-sticks in the form of a deer to test his son. He grants the Brahmana's fire-sticks back, promises that the Pandavas will spend their thirteenth year unrecognized in Virata's kingdom, and praises Yudhishthira's steadiness of virtue. The brothers wake refreshed and return the fire-sticks to the Brahmana, and the text closes with a promise of rewards for hearing this story. The passage ends the forest-exile test and sends the brothers into their year in disguise.

scenes.B03C312S01: The Yaksha reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira asks for the fire-sticks and a year of concealment, the god grants them, and the brothers return the fire-sticks to the Brahmana.

shots.B03C312S01H01: The brothers rise refreshed, and the Yaksha reveals himself as Yudhishthira's father, the Lord of justice, who had carried off the fire-sticks as a deer to test him; Yudhishthira asks that the Brahmana's worship of Agni not be interrupted.
shots.B03C312S01H02: The Yaksha grants that boon and offers another, and Yudhishthira asks that no one recognize the brothers during the thirteenth year.
shots.B03C312S01H03: The Yaksha grants that the brothers may spend the year unrecognized in Virata's kingdom and take any form they wish, and when Yudhishthira asks for steadiness against greed, anger and folly, the god says he already has those virtues.
shots.B03C312S01H04: The Lord of justice vanishes, the brothers wake and return to the hermitage to give the Brahmana his fire-sticks, and the text promises rewards to anyone who hears the tale.

B03C313.summary: Yudhishthira asks the ascetics for leave to spend the thirteenth year of exile in disguise and, overcome with grief, nearly faints. Dhaumya and Bhima encourage him with examples of gods and heroes who hid successfully and went on to win. The Brahmanas bless the Pandavas and leave, and the brothers set out with Krishna to plan their year of concealment. The rest of this chunk is the translator's footnotes and the Project Gutenberg license, which are not part of the epic's narrative.

scenes.B03C313S01: Yudhishthira asks leave to spend the thirteenth year in disguise, Dhaumya and Bhima encourage him, the Brahmanas depart, and the brothers set out to plan their year.
scenes.B03C313S02: Footnotes 4 to 8 explain rebirth, a grain plant, a translation choice, an asterism and a fragrant creeper.
scenes.B03C313S03: Footnotes 9 to 13 explain a passage on deathless life, a Vedic rite, the sale of the Vedas and silent recitation.
scenes.B03C313S04: Footnotes 14 to 18 explain mantras, the homa rite, a Vedic image, a word for discontent and a parting custom.
scenes.B03C313S05: Footnotes 19 to 23 explain the word karma, the role of Agni, Kartika, the offerings to gods and portions of the Vedas.
scenes.B03C313S06: Footnotes 24 to 28 explain love, Kama, the three uktha levels, a term for God, and the role of the Asuras in sacrifice.
scenes.B03C313S07: Footnotes 29 to 33 explain Mitra, a word for women, the sun's path, Raudra and the parable of Devasena.
scenes.B03C313S08: Footnotes 34 to 38 explain the personified anger, the name for gods, spirits, a royal ensign and Brahma.
scenes.B03C313S09: Footnotes 39 to 43 explain Devasenapati, two missiles, the word agrahara, and the army Krishna gave Duryodhana.
scenes.B03C313S10: Footnotes 44 to 48 explain Karna's vow, a small measure, two modes of gleaning, nakedness and two words in the Vedas.
scenes.B03C313S11: Footnotes 49 to 53 explain the six acts of a king, the constellation Mrigasiras, Varuna's abode, Garuda and Pavana.
scenes.B03C313S12: Footnotes 54 to 58 note textual variants, the achamana rite, a weapon, and burning wax-soaked brands used in siege.
scenes.B03C313S13: Footnotes 59 to 63 explain manhood and Rakshasas, two weapons, a medicinal plant, the Guhyakas, and the force of a Brahmana's curse.
scenes.B03C313S14: Footnotes 64 to 68 explain the muhurta and the asterism, Gayatri, killing, a word for letters, and a spiritual reading of the Yaksha's sun question.
scenes.B03C313S15: Footnotes 69 to 73 explain steadiness, a spiritual sacrifice, an alternative reading, air as the element, and the word for way.
scenes.B03C313S16: Footnotes 74 to 78 explain Vedic cosmology, the cow as food, the timing of Sraddha, and the lists of the five and six.
scenes.B03C313S17: The Project Gutenberg license heading that follows the text.

shots.B03C313S01H01: Yudhishthira asks the ascetics for leave to spend the thirteenth year in disguise, faints in grief, and is encouraged by Dhaumya's examples of gods who hid and won, and by Bhima's readiness to act; the Brahmanas bless them and leave, and the brothers set out with Krishna to take counsel.
shots.B03C313S01H02: Heading marking the end of the Vana Parva.
shots.B03C313S01H03: Footnote 1 lists six hazards to crops: excessive rain, drought, rats, locusts, birds and a hostile neighboring king.
shots.B03C313S01H04: Footnote 2 notes that the Sudras' rites have their origin in the Vedas.
shots.B03C313S01H05: Footnote 3 explains that the word for gods means a class of superhuman beings, distinct from the Supreme Spirit, and that virtuous people become such beings after death.
shots.B03C313S02H01: Footnote 4 explains the doctrine of the transmigration of souls.
shots.B03C313S02H02: Footnote 5 gives Wilson's suggestion that the Kora-dushakas grain is a Paspalum plant.
shots.B03C313S02H03: Footnote 6 explains the translator's coinage 'mlecchify' for a Sanskrit verb formed from a noun.
shots.B03C313S02H04: Footnote 7 explains Pushya as the eighth lunar asterism, made of three stars, linked to Cancer.
shots.B03C313S02H05: Footnote 8 identifies a creeper with large white fragrant flowers.
shots.B03C313S03H01: Footnote 9 says that those who live deathless lives can enjoy this bliss every day forever.
shots.B03C313S03H02: Footnote 10 notes that Vaka's answer does not seem to address Indra's question.
shots.B03C313S03H03: Footnote 11 describes the Swastivachana blessing rite and the flowery car that kings obtained from heaven.
shots.B03C313S03H04: Footnote 12 explains that a person who lectures on the Vedas for fees is said to sell them.
shots.B03C313S03H05: Footnote 13 defines japa as silent recitation of particular mantras.
shots.B03C313S04H01: Footnote 14 defines mantras as formulae of worship, often rhythmic and believed to be powerful.
shots.B03C313S04H02: Footnote 15 describes the homa as pouring clarified butter into fire.
shots.B03C313S04H03: Footnote 16 explains the phrase 'Vedamayi nou' as a boat made of the Vedas.
shots.B03C313S04H04: Footnote 17 explains the word vishada as discontent mixed with perplexity and confusion.
shots.B03C313S04H05: Footnote 18 describes a Hindu etiquette used at parting.
shots.B03C313S05H01: Footnote 19 notes that karma is hard to translate, since religion and morals were closely linked in Hindu thought.
shots.B03C313S05H02: Footnote 20 explains that Agni carried the oblations offered by people to the gods.
shots.B03C313S05H03: Footnote 21 explains that kumara means boy or prince and here means the war-god Kartika.
shots.B03C313S05H04: Footnote 22 explains that the oblations were carried to the gods.
shots.B03C313S05H05: Footnote 23 explains that the term refers to portions of the Vedas.
shots.B03C313S06H01: Footnote 24 says that raga means love.
shots.B03C313S06H02: Footnote 25 identifies Kama as the god of love, the Indian Cupid.
shots.B03C313S06H03: Footnote 26 explains the three ukthas as the body, the vivifying soul and the Supreme Spirit.
shots.B03C313S06H04: Footnote 27 says the term means the word of God.
shots.B03C313S06H05: Footnote 28 notes that Hindu mythology has no gods who destroy sacrifices, only Asuras, and compares the Zoroastrian view.
shots.B03C313S07H01: Footnote 29 notes that Mitra was the name of the chief god of the ancient Persians.
shots.B03C313S07H02: Footnote 30 explains that avala is a common name for women and means one without strength.
shots.B03C313S07H03: Footnote 31 explains that in Hindu belief the sun rises from one hill and sets behind another.
shots.B03C313S07H04: Footnote 32 explains that Raudra belongs to Rudra, the god of fury and war.
shots.B03C313S07H05: Footnote 33 explains Devasena as the celestial army and reads the story as an allegory of Indra seeking a leader.
shots.B03C313S08H01: Footnote 34 notes that anger personified is a deity.
shots.B03C313S08H02: Footnote 35 explains that the gods are so called because they have three stages of life and no old age.
shots.B03C313S08H03: Footnote 36 explains that the phrase means good and evil spirits.
shots.B03C313S08H04: Footnote 37 identifies an ensign of royalty in Hindustan.
shots.B03C313S08H05: Footnote 38 identifies the figure as Brahma.
shots.B03C313S09H01: Footnote 39 notes that Devasenapati can mean either the leader of the gods' army or the husband of Devasena.
shots.B03C313S09H02: Footnote 40 identifies the item as a kind of missile.
shots.B03C313S09H03: Footnote 41 identifies the item as another kind of weapon.
shots.B03C313S09H04: Footnote 42 explains agrahara as the food first taken from the stores after an offering, and notes that Draupadi always fed the Brahmanas first.
shots.B03C313S09H05: Footnote 43 explains the phrase as soldiers sworn to conquer or die, a full Akshauhini of whom Krishna gave to Duryodhana and who were all killed by Arjuna.
shots.B03C313S10H01: Footnote 44 gives the Burdwan pundits' view of the Asura vow and suggests that Karna took on Asura manners for his purpose.
shots.B03C313S10H02: Footnote 45 defines a term as a very small measure.
shots.B03C313S10H03: Footnote 46 explains the sila and unchha modes of life, which mean gleaning ears of corn or single grains left by harvesters.
shots.B03C313S10H04: Footnote 47 gives the meaning of the word as naked.
shots.B03C313S10H05: Footnote 48 notes that two words have doubtful meanings and in the Vedas denote knowledge and the moral sense.
shots.B03C313S11H01: Footnote 49 lists the six acts of a king: peace, war, marching, halting, sowing dissension and seeking protection.
shots.B03C313S11H02: Footnote 50 retells the story of Prajapati as a deer, struck down by Rudra, whose head became the constellation Mrigasiras.
shots.B03C313S11H03: Footnote 51 explains the phrase as the abode of Varuna.
shots.B03C313S11H04: Footnote 52 identifies the bird as Garuda.
shots.B03C313S11H05: Footnote 53 identifies Pavana as the wind god.
shots.B03C313S12H01: Footnote 54 notes a textual variant in which some editions read fifty-seven.
shots.B03C313S12H03: Footnote 56 explains the achamana purification rite, which Hindus still perform before any ceremony.
shots.B03C313S12H04: Footnote 57 explains the word as a rude engine, perhaps a primitive cannon.
shots.B03C313S12H05: Footnote 58 suggests the brands were wax-soaked torches thrown at the enemy, and compares a British siege at Bharatpore with burning cotton bales.
shots.B03C313S13H01: Footnote 59 explains that the phrase means be a man, which would not suit a Rakshasa.
shots.B03C313S13H02: Footnote 60 explains that this weapon restores a warrior to consciousness, while the Sam-mohana weapon makes one lose it.
shots.B03C313S13H03: Footnote 61 describes the Visalya plant as a healing plant for cuts and wounds, and reports a friend's test in which it stopped blood better than two acids.
shots.B03C313S13H04: Footnote 62 explains the Guhyakas as a class ranking just below the gods, and identifies the White mountain as Kailasa.
shots.B03C313S13H05: Footnote 63 explains that a Brahmana's curse is more terrible than Indra's thunderbolt, because it strikes a whole race.
shots.B03C313S14H01: Footnote 64 explains that Abhijit is the eighth muhurta of the day, about forty-eight minutes long, and identifies the asterism.
shots.B03C313S14H02: Footnote 65 identifies Savitri with Gayatri, the wife of Brahma.
shots.B03C313S14H03: Footnote 66 explains the word samhritya as killing.
shots.B03C313S14H04: Footnote 67 explains that the word means letters.
shots.B03C313S14H05: Footnote 68 gives a spiritual reading of the Yaksha's question about the sun, with answers pointing to Brahma, self-restraint, dharma and truth.
shots.B03C313S15H01: Footnote 69 explains dhriti as steadiness of intelligence and the word for second as a companion.
shots.B03C313S15H02: Footnote 70 gives a spiritual reading of the sacrifice, in which life, mind and prayerfulness take the place of the Sama, Yajus and Rik.
shots.B03C313S15H03: Footnote 71 notes an alternative reading and a spiritual reading of the words for those who offer to gods and to the Pitris.
shots.B03C313S15H04: Footnote 72 explains that Yudhishthira cites the Srutis for air as the one element that pervades the universe.
shots.B03C313S15H05: Footnote 73 explains that the word dik here means way, and that the way is the path of the good.
shots.B03C313S16H01: Footnote 74 notes that the Srutis speak of space as water and that these questions test Vedic cosmology.
shots.B03C313S16H02: Footnote 75 explains the Vedic chain by which the cow gives food, through milk, butter, homa, clouds and rain.
shots.B03C313S16H03: Footnote 76 explains that a Sraddha has no special time and may be held whenever a good priest is available.
shots.B03C313S16H04: Footnote 77 explains the five as tranquillity, self-restraint, abstention from sensual pleasures, resignation and yoga meditation.
shots.B03C313S16H05: Footnote 78 explains the six as hunger, thirst, sorrow, the loss of mortal feeling, decrepitude and death.
